title: Chief Sustainability Officers' Outlook September 2026
gist: A first-ever survey of 103 corporate chief sustainability officers in the World Economic Forum's global community finds 63% expect transition progress to hold steady or accelerate over the next year, with a stronger business case and cheaper, more applicable technologies cited as the leading medium-term accelerators. Policy uncertainty, short-term pressures and geopolitical volatility are making that progress uneven by market and sector, while sustainability migrates into commercial, operational and investment decisions and adaptation becomes a capital-allocation question.

themes.theme: Survey base rates on transition momentum

insights.claim: In a survey of 103 members of the World Economic Forum's global Chief Sustainability Officers Community, 63% expect progress on the transition to hold steady or accelerate over the next year.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A near two-thirds majority of corporate sustainability decision-makers expecting flat-to-faster progress argues against pricing a broad corporate retreat from transition capex; watch whether the 37% minority expecting deceleration grows in the next edition.
insights.quote: Overall, 63% expect progress to hold steady or accelerate over the next year
insights.locator: The inaugural Chief Sustainability Officers’ Outlook captures

insights.claim: The expected accelerators of corporate sustainability over the medium term are economic rather than regulatory: a stronger business case and cheaper, more applicable technologies lead the list.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Implies demand for clean/efficiency technology is increasingly tied to unit-cost curves and payback rather than subsidy or mandate, favouring suppliers whose products already clear an unsubsidized hurdle rate.
insights.quote: a stronger business case and cheaper, more applicable technologies are the leading expected accelerators
insights.locator: Overall, 63% expect progress to hold steady

insights.claim: Policy uncertainty, short-term pressures and geopolitical volatility are cited as the forces making transition progress more uneven across markets and sectors.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Dispersion, not direction, is the tradable variable: expect widening gaps between jurisdictions and sectors in transition-linked capex, which favours relative-value positioning over a single directional bet on the theme.
insights.quote: policy uncertainty, short-term pressures and geopolitical volatility are making progress more uneven across markets and sectors
insights.locator: At the same time, policy uncertainty

insights.claim: The central challenge identified for corporate sustainability leaders is building decisions that can withstand changing economic, political and geopolitical conditions, implying current sustainability plans are seen as fragile to regime change.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Durability-testing of sustainability commitments against political reversal becomes a screening criterion; commitments that only work under one policy regime are the ones most likely to be quietly dropped.
insights.quote: translating sustainability into decisions that create value, strengthen resilience and can withstand changing economic, political and geopolitical conditions
insights.locator: Across these themes, the report points to a central challenge

insights.claim: Sustainability is described as moving deeper into commercial, operational and investment decisions inside companies rather than sitting as a separate reporting or communications function.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: If the function is being absorbed into core P&L and capex decisions, standalone ESG-reporting and disclosure vendors face a weaker demand story than providers embedded in operations and procurement.
insights.quote: sustainability is moving deeper into commercial, operational and investment decisions
insights.locator: The outlook explores what this means inside companies

themes.theme: AI as capability and resource cost

insights.claim: AI is framed as offering new execution capabilities for corporate sustainability while simultaneously creating resource trade-offs, an explicitly two-sided view rather than a net positive.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Corporate sustainability leaders internalizing AI's energy and resource footprint is an early signal of procurement pressure on data-centre power sourcing and efficiency; watch for AI-related emissions becoming a named line in corporate targets.
insights.quote: AI offers new execution capabilities alongside resource trade-offs
insights.locator: The outlook explores what this means inside companies

insights.claim: Adaptation is becoming a core question of resilience and capital allocation for companies, marking a shift from emissions-reduction framing toward spending on withstanding physical and systemic shocks.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Adaptation and resilience spending is the under-owned leg of the theme relative to mitigation; watch for budget migration toward infrastructure hardening, water, cooling and insurance-adjacent services.
insights.quote: adaptation is becoming a core question of resilience and capital allocation
insights.locator: The outlook explores what this means inside companies

insights.claim: This is the inaugural edition of a recurring corporate sustainability outlook drawing on a defined community of sustainability leaders, creating a new baseline series for tracking corporate transition sentiment.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A first reading has no trend yet; its value is as a benchmark, so the 63% figure and the ranked accelerators are the numbers to diff against in the next edition.
insights.locator: From ambition to action: What chief sustainability officers see from the business frontline
